items.title: There are features in iPhone Duo that Apple didn't talk about
items.content_html:
Now that the iPhone Duo is at least partially out in the wild, the horde of reviewers that have used the device are finding things that were previously unannounced and undiscovered. Here are a few examples.

On September 9, Apple officially entered the folding smartphone market with its iPhone Duo. While customers won't be able to get their hands on one until October 23, select reviewers have already shared their thoughts on Apple's first foldable.

Alongside the usual opinions, many of these early reviews also detail obscure iPhone Duo features. For instance, when unfolded, the iPhone Duo supports Edge Light. In essence, the outermost area of the iPhone Duo's internal display acts as a ring light during FaceTime video calls.

This capability was previously exclusive to Macs with an Apple Silicon chip, which gained Edge Light with macOS Tahoe 26.2. This makes the iPhone Duo the first iPhone with Edge Light support. It's a nice touch for the foldable, but Edge Light is far from the only thing Apple customized for the iPhone Duo.

Because the iPhone Duo is similar in size to the iPad mini when unfolded, Apple opted to include a horizontal version of Reachability. Introduced in 2014, Reachability is an Accessibility feature that makes user interface elements near the top of an iPhone screen easier to access.

On the iPhone 6 and newer models, users can swipe down on the bottom edge of their iPhone screen to temporarily move the top of the iOS UI toward the lower half of the screen. This capability is available both on the iOS Home Screen and within applications.

With the iPhone Duo, the feature will seemingly work the same way, only with the left or right side of its displays. In essence, swiping towards the edge of the screen might move half of the on-screen UI to the left or right. Wired reports that the iPhone Duo will get reachability "later this year," per Apple.

Another capability launched with iPhone Duo is the Smart Take feature. Apple says the iPhone Duo "can detect when everyone is ready and takes the picture." This means no hassle with timers and no pushing buttons to take a picture with the iPhone Duo. It's also possible to use the outer display as a live viewfinder feed when taking photos.

Additionally, the iPhone Duo will gain Apple Pencil support with the upcoming iOS 27.2 update. The capability is already available with the release candidate build of iOS 27.2, which arrived on Monday.

However, while the iPhone Duo is undoubtedly full of useful product-specific UI enhancements, you'll only find them in Apple's apps, at least for the time being. Many third-party applications have yet to implement proper display support for the iPhone Duo's display aspect ratios.

As Engadget notes, many third-party apps viewed through the iPhone Duo's inner display only occupy the central area of the screen, leaving huge black bars on the right and left sides. Some applications, like Slack, however, have already addressed this issue.

Software-related details like these are eventually going to get fixed, but that won't be the case for the iPhone Duo's hardware. Some reviewers, like Arun Maini, have noted that desktop MagSafe chargers make the iPhone tip or rotate when the device is unfolded

Still, MagSafe is an entirely optional feature on the iPhone Duo. Apple's foldable can obviously be charged via USB-C, so the device won't tip over on its own. Overall, Apple still has a few kinks to work out with the iPhone Duo, and the product isn't for everyone, regardless of all the exclusive features it offers.

items.title: New PHP vulnerability means the Internet will have a very rough couple of days
items.content_html:
A severe vulnerability has been found in key web technology PHP, forcing just about everybody to patch websites, and fast. Expect outages.

Over the next couple of days, there will be more complaints about websites being down than usual. It's not just you, but the effects of the Internet relying on PHP and something going horrifically wrong.

The developers behind PHP, a web programming language, have said they will release a patch on Wednesday to fix a pair of vulnerabilities. They are rated at a very high 9.2 severity on the CVSSv4.0 severity scale.

The people behind the patch say that users should "upgrade as soon as the release is available," reports Reuters.

It is severe enough of a problem that EU cybersecurity officials have warned companies and organizations that can't apply the fixes must be prepared to take websites using PHP offline temporarily.

The EU Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) describes it as a risk of unauthenticated remote code execution. An attacker can insert code and run it on a vulnerable server.

The Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) has issued similar guidelines, advising to identify PHP servers and to apply patches, as well as to monitor for malicious activity.

While the ACSC wasn't aware of any active exploitation of the vulnerabilities, but Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said attacks were emerging. Cloudflare has updated its firewall rules as a temporary measure.

PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor or Personal Home Page) is a scripting language used in website development. It has been used for decades online, being one of the oldest technologies used to create interactive websites.

It is so popular that it has been used for many different platforms and purposes online, besides being used as a page scripting language.

Platforms including Drupal, Joomla, and Magneto heavily use PHP. So does WordPress, a blogging platform that is heavily used online by websites, including many that don't look like blogs.

In short, PHP runs many of the things that run the web, and this is a big problem.

This is a situation made worse by AI, which is being used to find vulnerabilities that hackers can exploit, or simply use AI to hack on their behalf.

End users do not have anything they can actually do about patching, unless they happen to have a personal web server using PHP. There are no patches needed for browsers or applications.

Really, all web users can do is hope that the patching and inevitable downtime don't take too long, and that the patches work.

You may want to keep a good book on standby to stave off boredom.

items.title: Critical PHP vulnerabilities threaten your NAS, not every vendor has a fix
items.content_html:
Attackers are actively exploiting critical PHP flaws to target internet-exposed NAS devices. If your files and backups are stored there, they're probably at risk.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a scripting language used by web servers and some NAS services. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, could allow attackers to execute code on affected servers without logging in.

The PHP development team released security updates on October 21 for versions 8.2 through 8.5. The urgency isn't hypothetical, as Amazon detected an attempted exploit on October 17, four days before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed.

For NAS owners, the threat affects both software maintained by the manufacturer and applications running independently in Docker containers. In either case, the risk of a remote attack depends on whether attackers can reach the vulnerable PHP service.

Synology has released updated PHP packages addressing the vulnerabilities. Its security advisory identifies PHP versions 7.3 through 8.4, Mail Station, and Synology Calendar among the affected products.

Updated PHP 8.2 and PHP 8.4 packages are available through Synology's Package Center and download archive. Owners should check the advisory for the status of other affected packages rather than assume every component has been patched.

Synology also distinguishes separately installed PHP packages from the PHP components built into DiskStation Manager. The manufacturer says its built-in PHP isn't exposed to external attack surfaces, making exploitation through that component unlikely.

QNAP confirmed a wider range of affected products in its October 22 advisory. The list includes QTS 5.2.11 and earlier, QTS 6.1.0, multiple versions of QuTS hero and QuTScloud, and applications such as Note Station 3.

The company is working on fixes but hasn't said when they will be available. QNAP reports no attacks targeting its products, though attempts to exploit vulnerable PHP servers have been documented.

Until patches arrive, QNAP recommends removing direct internet exposure by disabling unnecessary port forwarding, UPnP, and remote-access services. Owners who need remote connections should use a VPN and restrict management access to trusted networks.

Disabling the built-in web server can reduce exposure if the service isn't needed, but QNAP warns that doing so doesn't protect the NAS administration interface. Network restrictions remain necessary while the affected software is unpatched.

TerraMaster has acknowledged the problem in a Reddit discussion after an owner reported finding PHP 7.4.33 running the management interface on an F2-425 NAS.

In an October 22 response, TerraMaster said its team was investigating and testing the issue and working toward a fix. We haven't independently confirmed that the reported configuration is exploitable, and there is not yet a patch.

We also haven't been able to confirm whether Ugreen has released a PHP2Shell security update for UGOS Pro. The company's vulnerability policy describes how it handles security reports, but doesn't establish whether its NAS software is affected by these vulnerabilities.

Similarly, we couldn't confirm a PHP2Shell patch or a definitive affected-device list from Asustor. The manufacturer maintains a security advisory page, although the status of the specific vulnerability is listed as "ongoing."

NAS owners should check their manufacturer's security notices and available updates for their specific models.

Even a fully updated NAS operating system may still be running vulnerable PHP software inside Docker containers. These applications can include their own PHP installations, which aren't necessarily updated when the manufacturer patches the NAS firmware.

Owners running PHP-based services in Docker should check their container images for affected versions and install updated images as they become available. Applying an image update generally requires recreating the container so it runs the patched software.

QNAP explicitly warns that PHP installations inside Container Station and third-party applications aren't covered by its operating-system updates. The Dutch National Cyber Security Center also recommends identifying PHP installations in third-party software and applying the appropriate fixes.

If an affected container can't be updated immediately, owners should disable public access or restrict connections until a patch arrives. These measures reduce the risk of remote attacks but can't replace the security fixes recommended by PHP developers.

The greatest long-term concern involves older NAS hardware that no longer gets security updates. When manufacturer support ends, vulnerabilities can remain unpatched indefinitely, leaving owners exposed to known security problems beyond PHP2Shell.

An unsupported NAS can still provide local file storage, but exposing its administrative interface or other services directly to the internet creates unnecessary risk. Owners should remove public access rather than assume older hardware will eventually receive a fix.

Blocking unsolicited inbound connections keeps the device accessible locally while allowing outbound traffic for updates and other services.

For remote access, owners should use a secure VPN instead of forwarding NAS management ports. They should also check logs for suspicious activity, since updates won't undo an existing compromise.

items.title: Apps will be iPhone Duo's Achilles heel for now, no matter what Apple claims
items.content_html:
Apple has announced a slew of developers who have updated their apps to fit the iPhone Duo, but despite some surprises, there are still so many more who haven't had time.

Greg Joswiak has said he's proud of how well Apple managed to keep the iPhone Duo secret, and that did lead to there being so many surprises when it was announced. But it also meant that for the giant majority of developers, there has not been time to update their apps for the new device.

This is why amongst generally glowing reviews, two criticisms keep coming up. One is about the iPhone Duo's weight, which nothing can be done about, and the other concerns apps, which can be fixed.

Right now the majority of iPhone apps look a little squashed on the iPhone Duo's front screen. They also look a little lost in the middle of the opened-out inside screen.

This will change and not only will developers fit their apps to the iPhone Duo, they will find ways to exploit its new form. So the Omni Group, for instance, has its OmniFocus and OmniOutliner apps ready in compact form for the outer screen, and adapted to exploit the wide inner one.

Apple itself has redone its own apps for the iPhone Duo, when it still hasn't for the Apple Vision Pro years after that launched. And now Apple has shown off more third-party apps that are also ready.

"The response to iPhone Duo from our developer community has been incredible," Susan Prescott, Apple's vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, said in a statement, "and we're inspired by how quickly they've embraced its larger display and new ways to interact."

"From watching popular shows and content on the expansive inner display to multitasking across windows or playing console-quality games, developers around the world are reimagining what their apps can do," she continued. "We can't wait for users to discover these experiences beginning this Friday, with many more app experiences to follow."

Powerful To Do app OmniFocus has been updated to give an expanded widescreen view (left) and a new compact one for the iPhone Duo's front screen (right) - image credit: Omni Group.

The apps that Apple picks out include ones it has already shown, such as Netflix. But it's also said that other video apps are coming:

"People watch Netflix in all kinds of moments, and we built our new experience to move with them," Netflix's senior director of Engineering, Tom Richards, said. "From browsing Clips on the outer display to settling in with a favorite show on the inner display, the experience adapts as iPhone Duo opens, closes, or turns, so discovering something new and sitting down to watch it feels effortless."

Then some key productivity apps like Bear, Things, and Notewise have been updated. Plus there are longtime Mac and iPhone developers such as Flexibits, the maker of Fantastical and Cardhop:

"Fantastical has always been about seeing your day at a glance, and iPhone Duo gives us more room to do that than any iPhone before it," Flexibits CEO Michael Simmons said. "With calendars, tasks, and menus visible together on the inner display, it feels like the full Fantastical experience from Mac and iPad, right in your pocket."

Given their history on Apple platforms, you would expect Fantastical and the Omni apps to be ready promptly. But if you've been around Apple long enough, there are apps you'd think might never come.

Yet they have. Netflix is one, since the company will seemingly never support the Apple TV app, despite tantalizing hints it will.

But the real surprise is that Microsoft is on board with the iPhone Duo. Apple says that both Microsoft Word and Microsoft Outlook will come to the iPhone Duo in the coming weeks.

Fantastical has been updated for the iPhone Duo - image credit: Apple/Flexibits.

That Microsoft is coming at all is good, given how it delayed supporting the iPad for several years. In that case, what kept Microsoft away was seemingly that it believed it could prevent the iPad becoming a success.

So the fact that Microsoft is supporting the iPhone Duo is excellent. Except there is that matter of it taking another few weeks.

If developers followed all of Apple's strong recommendations about coding their apps in certain ways for the last few years, they'd be in great shape. They'd genuinely not have an immense amount more to do to perfectly exploit the iPhone Duo's screen size, if not its extra features.

But Apple will never say why it is recommending something. Although savvy developers can often guess, it's also never for a reason that is urgent.

Apple may see it as giving developers time, but instead it's always giving them a dilemma.

Zenless Zone Zero has been updated too - image credit: Apple/Zenless Zone Zero

Developers have to decide whether and when to devote resources to reworking their apps to fit Apple, or to add new features. Typically reworking an app means affecting things users never see, so there will always be a pressure to do the more visible work.

Then, too, one of the reasons that Microsoft is a surprise is that it is a huge company. You might expect that a large firm would be better able to adapt apps than a one-man or one-woman band, but it may not be.

A lone developer can make the choice to support something and work on it immediately. A large firm will have its own goals for its apps and will have teams working toward release schedules.

For them, choosing to support new Apple features means pushing back their own plans. It also means liaising with multiple team members across departments from coding to marketing, where each already has their hands full.

If you were waiting to order an iPhone Duo, the time between its announcement on September 9, 2026, and its at least partial availability on October 23, seems like an eternity. But even with generative AI assistance and similar tools it is not nearly enough time for every developer to work through plans and update their apps.

That's especially so because with the exception of firms whose apps were shown at the launch, few or no developers had an iPhone Duo to try. Even those developers who began work immediately, couldn't actually submit their apps to Apple until October 8.

Plus it wasn't until a week after the launch that Xcode was updated to let developers build iPhone Duo apps. Even then, they could run it in the Xcode simulator, but nothing beats testing your software on actual devices.

So the job became understanding the differences with the iPhone Duo, redesigning and coding apps to fit that, then producing the apps. And then submitting to the App Store and hoping the app gets passed in time for the first real users on October 23.

Consequently, there will be developers who have simply decided not to do anything until they could get an iPhone Duo or three. There will be others who were racing to be ready for October 23, and simply couldn't make it.

And there will be still other developers who will never update their apps for the iPhone Duo.

The good thing is that most developers will, and also that for them and us as users, it is only a matter of time. If your pre-ordered iPhone Duo isn't coming until January 2027, you may well never see an app that isn't updated for it.

items.title: Australia demands Apple make DMA-like changes to App Store by March 2027
items.content_html:
After years of litigation, Apple has been told by the Federal Court of Australia to allow alternative App Stores and end anti-steering practices, basically copying previous rulings.

Apple is facing antitrust lawsuits and similar battles around the world. The EU has forced a lot of change to the Apple App Store thanks to the Digital Markets Act, and it seems the Australian government wants similar action through a single piece of legislation.

According to the 1,104-paragraph filing, Apple has engaged in antitrust conduct that warrants remedial action. The demands made are similar in scope to the EU's DMA, though with some specificity to prevent any wiggle room from Apple.

First, Apple must allow Epic to resubmit Fortnite and any other apps to the App Store, provided they follow Apple's current guidelines. It seems this resubmission is expected to occur immediately.

In addition, the following demands are being made by the Australian Federal Court:

Apple must have these orders completed by March 1, 2027. It has until February 15, 2027 to submit evidence of why it might need an extension if it isn't ready by February 1.

The court also says Apple owes 85% of Epic's costs for the trial. As always, Apple is expected to appeal every step of the way.

items.title: AI audio firm Samplab acquired by Apple to boost Logic Pro
items.content_html:
Apple has acquired AI audio editing firm Samplab, likely to extend Logic Pro's existing stem splitting tools, as well as adding the ability to edit individual notes in chords.

Following its deal with the Huxe AI podcast company, Apple has now acquired Zurich-based Samplab under a similar arrangement. As detailed in the European Union's public list of acquisitions, Apple is to acquire certain assets, and offer employment to certain Samplab employees.

Samplab was founded in Hauptsitz, Zurich, Switzerland, in 2020 by Manuel Fritsche and Gian-Marco Hutter. It's believed to have no more than 10 employees and based on LinkedIn profiles, may even only employ the two founders.

The company has previously described itself as being about "music production for the age of AI." Before being closed down, its official website promoted how its software could "change any note in your audio," and "detect and edit chords."

Samplab's software also included what the firm described as granular stem separation. Since 2024, Apple's Logic Pro has had stem splitting, which uses AI to isolate vocals, guitars, drums, and so on, into separate tracks.

The company's software was available as a plugin for Digital Audio Workstations (DAW), including Logic Pro. So while neither Samplab nor Apple have commented publicly, it seems most probable that the firm's technology will be used in Apple Creator Studio and Logic Pro.

Samplab's notice to existing users before its website was rerouted to Apple's - image credit: Samplab.

According to the EU, Apple made this deal through an unnamed subsidiary on June 17. In late June, Samplab's official website posted that it was closing down, and would be refunding subscribers with the remainder of their annual subscription fee.

That official site now routes through to apple.com. Other links to Samplab plugins are currently routing to a "page not found" on Apple's site.

Samplab's Twitter channel appears to have been gutted, and its YouTube channel has definitely had its videos removed.

This acquisition is the latest of several reported to the EU, with most being small firms such as Samplab, Huxe, and Prompt AI. It bought Q.Ai in January 2026 for an estimated $2 billion, however, and reportedly may be working to make other large-scale acquisitions.

items.title: Apple Vision Pro with M5 review one year later: Signs of life in a platform on hold
items.content_html:
After a year of use, it remains clear that the Apple Vision Pro benefits from the power of M5, even if not much else changed. Apple's work is far from over.

I'm writing this review with ten Safari tabs open in a carousel, Drafts below, Music in a mini player on my right, and various social apps behind me. The Apple Vision Pro with M5 isn't showing signs of strain, and that's even with visionOS 27 running as I write some portions of this review.

It shouldn't be. It's M5 after all.

Anyway. The Apple Vision Pro is a complicated device to discuss.

It still feels magical every time I put it on, but the software other than the OS is nearly identical to where it was one or even two years ago.

Apple Vision Pro continues to be an amazing piece of technology three years after its reveal during WWDC 2023, and one year into M5, everything feels new again.

Neglect from developers and Apple itself has left Apple Vision Pro in a software quagmire. Since my previous review, Apple Creator Studio came and went with no apps for Apple Vision Pro, no iPad-compatible apps offered by Apple have become native, and the only new app is the Siri AI app introduced with visionOS 27.

Apple Vision Pro review: still a great productivity tool

Layoffs have impacted Apple Vision Pro's gaming and immersive video teams, and there are no signs of release pacing for either product increasing. It's all on external studios and developers to keep pushing out Vision Pro-specific content, and there's just no money in it.

To top it all off, the Apple Vision Pro is now even more expensive at $3,699 thanks to AI-driven RAM shortages.

To any outside observer reading those preceding paragraphs, things look bleak for Apple Vision Pro. Matters are even more dire when you account for the fact that new Apple CEO John Ternus is allegedly not a fan of the product.

Apple Vision Pro review: the Dual Knit band might be enough to help some people be comfortable

All that said, I don't think Apple has given up on the Apple Vision Pro just yet. It's still selling in some limited fashion, the users that love it do love it a lot, and new apps are being built, if slowly.

This review might look a little different from my other Apple Vision Pro reviews. So much ink has already been spilled on these subjects, and given the stagnant nature of the platform, there isn't much to add. Unfortunately.

So, one year after the Apple Vision Pro M5 release, let's get into the state of it in late 2026.

We've already highlighted the state of the platform from a wider corporate view, many times, so let's get into the hardware itself. As it stands in late 2026, my opinion hasn't wavered — Apple Vision Pro is unmatched.

Apple Vision Pro review: no competing headset comes close

But wait, I just spent several paragraphs basically spelling out the epitaph of Apple's expensive headset. Sure, that is a reality we have to face for the platform today, but none of that affects how Apple Vision Pro works or feels.

Apple Vision Pro has been an accomplishment in the market, and you can tell just by looking at the competition. Android XR, Meta Quest, and others have pursued visionOS-like layouts, gestures, and features since Apple's headset hit the market.

None of them come close to the fidelity provided by Apple Vision Pro. They're all pursuing it on lesser hardware, and some come close, but they can't quite get there without significantly increasing the price of the hardware itself.

Some have suggested that this means Apple should have made a headset with lower specs and a lower price tag. However, this ignores the fact that the headset market itself is quite limited as it is, and another in the competing sub $1,000 price bracket would be virtually ignored.

The M5 version didn't change much. It swapped out the M2 for the M5 and introduced the new Dual Knit band.

The M5 is noticeably more powerful given it can drive the full resolution of the included displays at a higher refresh rate. Widgets aren't left in a blank state as you turn your head as often, and apps don't crash in the background either.

The Dual Knit band helps make the weight of the Apple Vision Pro mostly ignorable for me. I can wear it for hours at a time without needing a break for neck fatigue, though my eyes do need a rest from time to time like with any display.

Apple Vision Pro review: if Apple's bands don't work, try a third-party option

I never had an issue with the Solo Knit band and didn't like the Dual Loop band for the original Apple Vision Pro. I've tested the ResMed and CMA1 alternative bands, and each offered their own ways to manage the Apple Vision Pro's weight.

Counterweights only increased the total weight load on your head and neck, and alternative pads helped with weight distribution, but never felt overly premium. They helped some folks find a good fit, but they never worked for me.

The Dual Knit band ended up being the perfect solution. It has such a wide surface area that I'm almost wearing a helmet. The top strap keeps the Apple Vision Pro basically suspended above my nose while the rear band keeps the pressure distributed around my temples.

Of course, everyone's fit and comfort will be different. You'll have to find what works for you.

Thankfully, the software needed to do my job has been there since the start. I write in Drafts, I research and publish in Safari, and I use Indigo and Tapestry for watching for new stories.

Apple Vision Pro review: a new Safari tab view in visionOS 27

I do wish more of these apps were native Apple Vision Pro ones, but the iPad-compatible versions are good enough. Placing the windows and widgets around my office still feels fun and whimsical in a way even iPad can't match.

The Apple Vision Pro continues to be the best place to view almost any kind of media. It elevates simple still photos, adds depth to panoramas, and makes every video into a movie theater.

My collection of 3D movies in the Apple TV keeps growing, and Apple Immersive Video gets new content from time to time. Apple's work in the sports industry has even brought some interesting features to life, like watching an NBA or MLB game live in immersive.

I guess Apple Vision Pro might be the only place outside of theaters to watch The Odyssey in the glorious IMAX format. It would be a waste if Apple doesn't find a way to make it happen.

Apple Vision Pro review: watching MLB games in immersive format is amazing

Of course, I mean this should be present in the Apple TV app as a version purchasable from the Apple TV Store. There is an IMAX app on Apple Vision Pro, but it's essentially dead, and I'd prefer not have a purchased movie siloed there anyway.

It's easy to look at the snail's pace progress of Apple Vision Pro and get frustrated. It's an expensive piece of hardware that's seen very little budge in the past few years.

However, as Tim Cook said, Apple knew Vision Pro would be for a niche audience that wanted to glimpse the future of computing. No one knows Apple's success targets for the platform or what things look like as it moves forward.

Apple is a weird company inside and out. It doesn't operate like other companies, so trying to apply the same logic to Apple that you might other companies doesn't always work.

Apple Vision Pro might be on its way out for all we know, but there are enough signs to suggest otherwise. It's quite possibly the worst the platform will ever be, and that's saying something considering how great it is today.

As good as the hardware is, I can't ignore the state of things in software. This isn't a review of visionOS, you've already got that from me this year.

When I say software, I mean the app ecosystem. Imagine if iPad didn't get a notable new app in a year. That is essentially where we are with Apple Vision Pro, minus some vibecoded software that mostly needs to be sideloaded.

Don't get me wrong, there are new apps for Apple Vision Pro, and some even appear interesting. Some of the very few new games are interesting, but none capture my attention long.

Gaming on Apple Vision Pro is precisely where I left it a year ago. Thrasher got a remastered update with PSVR2 support and better visuals, but that's the only one that seems to have done such an update.

Apple Vision Pro review: gaming has barely budged in a year

Most of the games on my Apple Vision Pro have no update history or updates from two years ago. The few that do show recent updates within a few months are bug fixes or basic changes.

Apple Arcade might be the only place gaming actually exists on Apple Vision Pro, and given the layoffs, that may soon stop. Developers will have to bring games to Apple Vision Pro on their own, and I don't see an incentive to do so.

The other side of this is game streaming. Whether it's via NVIDIA GeForce Now or a custom-built PC, streaming VR to Apple Vision Pro is one of the best ways on the market to interact with that content.

Apple Vision Pro review: a great gaming companion even without many games on the platform

Sure, Apple Vision Pro is heavy, but for flight simulators like X-Plane 12, it's perfect for immersion. Developers can even develop special controllers that remain visible when fully immersed and track to game environments.

Those with an expensive iRacing rig can also take advantage of the high resolution and frame rates offered by Apple Vision Pro. iVRY is another option for those that already have a VR gaming library on a capable Windows gaming PC.

The app situation isn't much better. I browse the Apple Vision Pro App Store from time to time to find very little has changed.

Apple Vision Pro review: productivity apps haven't budged in a year

Apple's editors almost never write new "Today" stories or roundups. Very few apps are for productivity, instead several focus on single-use experiences like viewing objects in space.

It's not that those kinds of apps aren't welcome, but they hardly help make Apple Vision Pro more viable as a platform. What's worse is Apple's total absence from the story.

I still can't edit photos on Apple Vision Pro without a third-party app or Mac Virtual Display. While I love that I can bring my Mac into the virtual view, it's more of an escape hatch than anything.

Apple Vision Pro review: Siri AI is useful but not a productivity suite

There are also some odd decisions in Apple Vision Pro I still don't understand. Find My doesn't exist in any form, locking windows doesn't matter if you accidentally invoke the app elsewhere, and keyboards still disappear when fully immersed unless you buy Apple's.

It's a weird platform with plenty of quirks and rough edges to smooth out, but even then, it's industry-leading. Every new OS brings new ideas, bug fixes, and streamlined features.

I'll chalk most of this up to growing pains as Apple prepares for what's next in spatial computing. None of this means Apple Vision Pro is bad or dead, nor does it mean Apple has abandoned the product.

It's a weird time to be a fan of Apple Vision Pro. Pundits can't help but declare it dead at least once a month and Apple's internal shifts don't help matters.

Regardless of what conjecture can be made or small details leak out, Apple has a near-infinite cash runway for toying around with projects regardless of how successful they might be. Apple Vision Pro could truly be a money sink for Apple, but their priorities for the future mean that it doesn't matter.

I'm confident that spatial computing is what's next in computing, at least as an alternative platform. The iPad previously represented a future of computing that's still taking shape, but visionOS looks out even further than that.

See, at one point we believed that computing would be terminal-based where your account existed no matter which device you sat down at. That ultimately came to pass thanks to the internet and cloud-based accounts.

Apple Vision Pro review: hardware that's ahead of its time

The iPad took that idea and flipped it. Instead of many access terminals with multiple powerful computers, you have one computer, a naked robotic core, and transport it between terminals that have no computer present.

Whatever accessory you attach to the iPad transformed it into the computer you needed, be it a gaming console, writing terminal, laptop, sketchpad, or reading tablet — it did it all.

Apple Vision Pro removes the terminal altogether, though there will be times you'll want a classic keyboard and trackpad setup. Spatial computing means that the computer appears wherever you might be looking whenever you need it, which means the compute unit is worn on the person instead of being carried.

It takes the naked robotic core concept and kind of turns it inside out. It no longer involves attaching accessories to create the computing environment you need, but using accessories to attach information.

Once visionOS can find its way into a routinely wearable AR display, we'll see a hybrid reality where iPhones and iPads are still used, but the AR view can extend content outside of the physical glass. Apple Vision Pro is the first step in that direction because it fakes the AR we're aiming for.

Apple Vision Pro review: glasses are Apple's goal

Apple Vision Pro needed to release and exist so Apple could develop visionOS in public. It needed an audience of users and developers at a scale wider than those found at Apple Park to push the technology forward.

In the short term, I believe Apple has accomplished what it wanted with Apple Vision Pro. The M5 model likely only exists because enough people, especially enterprise, still buy the headset and Apple didn't want to make another batch of M2 chips, given the state of the chipmaking industry right now.

It isn't as if Apple merely slapped the chipset in and called it a day. Work had to go into optimizing the hardware for the new chip beyond simple speed increases.

Apple Vision Pro review: chipset upgrades helped push the platform forward and keep it modern

Real advantages were gained because of the chip upgrade, and more benefits can be found in AI, gaming, and graphics applications as time moves forward. Even the Developer Strap saw a speed upgrade for tethered operations.

I don't think we'll see another iteration of this headset, though rumors have been wishy-washy on the topic. Apple will inevitably create the next-generation model with a thinner, lighter frame that is hopefully marginally less expensive.

Such a device is coming. Patents and rumors continue to point to such a product being in the pipeline, but component suppliers can't meet the need just yet.

Even Sony struggled to make enough displays for the initial product launch. That's just how far ahead the Apple Vision Pro was in 2024 and continues to be today.

Apple Vision Pro review: It's just the beginning of Apple's spatial computing platform

Until the technology can catch up to Apple's ambitions, I think it makes sense to redistribute engineers to more imminent products. Clearly, in its current form, software, gaming, and immersive video aren't worth the effort for the audience size, so downsizing there makes some sense too.

That doesn't mean we won't see new content for those categories, just less direct from Apple. Really, we don't even know who was laid off. It could have been product managers, engineers, or even just evangelists — it's only about 60 people in a team of hundreds.

For now, Apple is pushing for smart glasses and AirPods with cameras. Both products will benefit from more development in AI and spatial computing, even if they don't run visionOS directly.

Rumors place a next-generation Apple Vision Pro somewhere around 2028 or early 2029. I'll continue to cover visionOS releases and point out specific upgrades and apps as they come in.

The Mac is a powerhouse capable of doing most anything you throw at it. Developers, writers, movie producers, and most anyone can do their work with a Mac.

Apple Vision Pro review: for the crazy ones

Go down a rung and you're at iPad. For most it's a consumption device, but for a slice of the Apple-faithful population, it's a more whimsical production platform that's way more interesting than a Mac. Our naked robotic core.

Then there's Apple Vision Pro. It's truly the device for the crazy ones, especially if you buy one today at $3,699.

If Apple Vision Pro with M5 warrants another review check in, I'll be here, hopefully with some good news. Until then, I'll continue to put on Apple Vision Pro on a regular basis to relive memories, watch 3D movies, and play the occasional game.

Oh, and of course, get some work done. This entire review was written while wearing the Apple Vision Pro and my neck doesn't even hurt.

My pros and cons didn't change much in the past year, but neither did the platform. visionOS 27 is a great step forward, but all of my concerns for the platform continue to be unaddressed.

The rating dropped to represent the continued lack of developer support and the higher price tag. Those that need or want Apple Vision Pro likely already have one, and I'm not sure how far this platform will move forward in the intervening years between now and the next hardware update.

We'll be back to discuss things further as soon as there's an update worth discussing.

The M5 Apple Vision Pro is available for purchase at Apple.com, with a starting price of $3,699. You can also check out the secondhand market on eBay.com for deals on pre-owned M2 models.

items.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for lying to users about privacy
items.content_html:
A New Mexico judge hit Meta with a record-breaking $25 billion penalty on Wednesday, stemming from a lawsuit over the Cambridge Analytica debacle.

The ruling follows September's guilty finding after a two-week trial. Ultimately, the court ruled that Meta was responsible for 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer privacy laws.

Each charge carried a penalty of up to $5000, leading to the record-breaking sum. Judge Francis J. Mathew of the Santa Fe State District Court made the ruling.

And this is on top of about $950 million in damages assessed earlier in the year after the state's judiciary found the social media giant liable for harms to children.

Also in 2026, the company negotiated a $17.1 billion settlement the company in August with 47 states, Washington DC, and other US territories. New Mexico led its own charge against the company and did not get involved in that case, nor its settlement.

The parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp has generated about $168.6 billion in profit over the trailing twelve months.

Meta's earnings are after the market closes on Wednesday, just hours after this announcement. The company has not replied to a request for comment from the New York Times yet, but it will certainly get asked some during that event.

Facebook has previously been fined $5 billion over the issue by the Federal Trade Commission.

Speaking in 2018, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that he had been "working to understand exactly what happened and how to make sure this doesn't happen again." Four years later, it's still not yet clear what the company has gleaned from the experience.

At around the same time, Apple's Tim Cook criticized the privacy failing, and said that it meant the time was past for companies to be allowed to entirely self-regulate.

"I think the best regulation is no regulation, is self-regulation," he said at the time, in answer to a question posed about Facebook. "However, I think we're beyond that here."

In 2023, there was a class-action payout from a $725 million settlement about the issue. The claim period is long past, and people in the US who used Facebook between May 24, 2007, and December 22, 2022, were eligible to receive a payment.

items.title: Apple Music's gorgeous rebrand leans on Liquid Glass
items.content_html:
Apple has revealed how it used music itself to create the visuals for its new Apple Music rebrand that features a "made by sound" rippling visual sting.

First Apple remade its Apple Music logo into a more chunky design, then it unveiled a new visual identity at the opening of its Apple Music Hall in Battersea, London. Now in a new video, Apple has revealed how months of work went into the design.

"For the rebrand of Apple Music, we wanted sound to create the visuals," says the narrator of Apple's new video. "How do we take this idea of music and distill it into something visually beautiful? Essentially the idea was to create the perfect sound wave."

Apple Music partnered with British producer Fred Again... and NEST Acoustics to create a visual identity formed from sound.

"We take a frequency and we play it through a rig [which] then moves a large amount of liquid at the frequency of the notes," continues the narration. "We partnered with one of the world's best music artists to create the notes for the final mnemonic, and then we use that sound to create the visuals."

An Apple Music logo was etched into the glass floor of a small tank, and that was then filled with mineral oil. A transparent cover in the shape of an app icon was placed over the logo, and on the moving rig.

Then when a short series of tones, specially chosen for this work, were played, a transducer vibrated. It sends the oil rippling out from the rig and distorting the Apple Music logo.

That footage will now be used as a short sting introducing Apple Music videos. A version with just the two-note logo instead of any text is also to be overlaid at the start of Apple Music footage such as concert videos.

Both versions are very reminiscent of Apple's Liquid Glass redesign. Plus the fact that it was done in-camera with a practical effect instead of CGI is just as Apple did for its Apple TV rebrand in November 2025.

items.title: Don't return an unexpected Apple Cash payment, it's a scam
items.content_html:
That Apple Cash payment you got from a stranger is not a mistake and the sob story they tell begging you to return it is just part of the con. Here's how to protect yourself.

You almost have to give scammers credit for ingenuity. Someone figured out how to profit from sending a stranger an iPhone, and now someone has found a way to manipulate Apple Cash users.

As happened to a Reddit user, the first thing is that you get an unexpected payment appearing on your iPhone in the Apple Cash part of Apple Wallet. It doesn't matter if you don't already use Apple Cash, as all that will happen is that you're prompted to set it up.

That setup prompt is Apple's and it is legitimate, because the payment appears to be too. If you're not expecting this payment and you haven't already setup Apple Cash, though, save yourself some time by declining the payment.

If you are a user already then by default, this payment will just go into your Apple Cash account. Then very shortly afterwards, if not immediately, you get a message asking you to please return it.

Doubtlessly, many people will just do that. If you hesitate even a little, the message ramps up the pressure.

First you're told it was a mistake, they meant to send it to someone else, but then they start getting really detailed.

Typically they'll say something about how the money was meant to go to something to do with their children. It'll have been for a basketball lesson or something, and if you still don't return the money, now you get sobbing emojis and a claim that it was the sender's last dime.

It's all to make you believe that returning the money is urgent, and so stop you having time to think about it.

What's really happening is that while, yes, you have received money, it was fraudulent. The issuing bank will eventually reverse the payment when, for instance, it's shown that it came from a stolen credit card.

So instead of a seemingly simple return of someone's cash, you will instead have paid them that cash out of your own money.

If you're reading this because it's currently happening to you, do not engage with the scammer's messages any further. Instead, try this first:

There won't be a Reject Payment button if you have already accepted the payment, though. And you may well have done that, as Apple Cash is set to automatically accept incoming payments from any source.

In that case, ignore or block any messages from this scammer and know that the payment will eventually vanish.

You can also turn off this automatic acceptance of payments to prevent this happening in future.

From then on, any time anyone sends you a payment, you will have to tap an Accept button to receive it. You'll have seven days in which to accept the payment.

This particular scam appears to be quite new, but the more people use digital wallets and digital payments, the more fraud attempts there will be. Most recently, scammers have been pretending Apple Pay payments have been declined, for instance.

items.title: Apple blocks bafflingly weak internet security certificates on iPhone
items.content_html:
Apple has blocked on iOS and iPadOS a set of eight compromised security certificates that were found to be astoundingly weak. It's a bit more complicated on Mac.

Security certificates (SSL/TLS) are used to keep Internet users secure, thanks to using encryption to secure traffic and to verify domain ownership. However, a collection of certificates from one authority has been pulled from use after security researchers found them to be extremely weak.

As a result, Indian certificate authority eMudhra revoked the certificates. This prevents the certificates from being used by websites, closing the barn door after their discovery and disclosure on October 17.

According to Beeping Computer, Google Chrome blocked a set of six compromised intermediates authorized to issue TLS certificates. Meanwhile Mozilla blocked compromised certificates in Firefox.

While Google and Mozilla instigated the blocks on October 17, Apple was a little later in doing so. It added protections in iOS and iPadOS on October 19.

It's not so simple on Mac. More on that in a bit.

The point of a security certificate is that it can let systems identify each other and set up encryption between the two points. That encryption requires the creation of keys, both to set up and to decrypt the data.

This key is usually lengthy and complex, to a level that it would take way too much effort to guess the key or determine it by brute-forcing every possible combination, in a reasonable timeframe. Think along the lines of keys over 100 characters long.

In this instance, the keys for the eight certificates were entirely guessable, even by humans. The compromised private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

For clarity, those numbers aren't the lengths of keys. Those are the actual keys for each of the eight certificates.

This is on a par with using a system password of "password" or "123" and hoping it doesn't get guessed.

According to Mozilla's bug reporting system, Mozilla was able to recover the private keys very easily. And the keys were recovered without any prior knowledge of how the original reporter did it.

Of those eight certificates, six were used for TLS, and were trusted by Apple, Chrome, Microsoft, and Mozilla root programs. The other two are used for code signing and trusted by Microsoft.

Further complicating matters is that these certificates were generated in April 2025, so they have been available for well over a year. However, most of the certificates didn't make it into production, and there's no evidence of attackers recovering or using the keys either.

When it comes to what end users need to do, the advice is fairly simple: update your software as soon as you can. In some cases, like Mozilla's inclusion of the OneCRL system in Firefox, the protections were implemented without requiring a browser update or even a restart.

For Apple users, that means updating their apps, as well as iOS and macOS.

Mac users do still have to be wary, as the built-in curl utility doesn't check revocation information. If the Mac has encountered and trusted the certificates in the past, it will blindly continue to do so going forward.

That said, the assurance that most weren't use and the insistence that attackers haven't taken advantage of it may mean that few Mac users, if any, will be affected.

For eMudhra, in a statement on the matter, it insists there was no infrastructure compromise nor signs of any data breaches. It is also working with customers who may have been affected to replace the certificates.

items.title: Apple CEO John Ternus says design still means everything & includes whimsey
items.content_html:
"Design is how it works" rings true at Apple today, and John Ternus wants to assure everyone that respect for the user and building products that are beneficial is "job one."

John Ternus may be Apple's new CEO but he's not letting his new role interrupt his passion for industrial design. He emphasized that Apple had been working towards iPhone Duo for over 15 years in a previous interview.

A video version of that interview with Time was shared Tuesday with more conversation around the importance of design at Apple. Ternus starts by sharing his continued role of being involved with industrial design.

John Ternus joined Apple 25 years ago as a member of the product design team. His background in mechanical engineering placed him close to the industrial design team.

"I think what's so special about this place is design is at the center of it," Ternus shared. "Our designers both on the software side and the hardware side, they really understand the engineering. And the engineers have a deep appreciation for design."

"It's a really powerful collaboration," he concluded.

The conversation touched on similar topics in the previous published article, like child safety, Screen Time, and Ternus' love of driving fast cars. Everything centered around the announcement of the iPhone Duo and it representing Apple's ability to provide something useful while being whimsical.

"I think the opportunities in the products, that stuff will change," Ternus said in response to a question about Apple's future emphasis on design. "It'll evolve as it does as new technologies come, but the way we work — I don't want that to change."

Apple has notably sat out the larger portion of the AI race by not developing its own frontier model. Apple's executives have shared that the company doesn't need to develop everything, nor does it need to appeal to a "lunatic fringe."

"Design has always been at the core of this company, and I think our respect for the user and for building products that are helpful and beneficial to people — that is job one," Ternus concluded. "We're going to continue on that."

Apple ships the iPhone Duo to the lucky customers that managed to pre order one for release on October 23. The device has reportedly seen "extraordinary demand" and new orders won't ship until the end of January 2027.

items.title: Perplexity Computer can run completely local on Mac, with a big caveat
items.content_html:
Perplexity Computer now runs entirely on Apple Silicon Macs, but its recommended RAM requirement is pretty steep and limits actual deployments.

The fully local mode launched October 20 for Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. The release builds on April's Personal Computer launch and September's Hybrid Compute update. Personal Computer brought AI automation to native Mac apps, while Hybrid Compute paired local processing with cloud-based reasoning.

Users can now choose to keep an entire task on their Mac or authorize cloud processing when additional capabilities are needed. That is, assuming the minimum requirements are met.

The fully local version of Computer supports Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro, a Perplexity-trained version of Qwen. Both models run on the Mac, handling reasoning and coordinating tasks without relying on remote AI servers.

With permission, Computer can work across native apps including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers. Rather than simply generating text, the agent can collect information, modify documents, and complete tasks involving several apps.

Perplexity says Computer can review messages and emails, identify outstanding deadlines, and create a task list in Notes. It can also analyze private financial information against downloaded market data, update an Excel workbook, and prepare a Keynote presentation for review.

Code execution and tool operations take place in isolated sandbox environments, according to Perplexity, with controlled access to files and supported apps. Users can also authorize Computer to access cloud services for current information, browser use, connected apps, and advanced reasoning using more than 15 frontier models.

Fully local processing doesn't necessarily make every workflow independent of the internet. Sending an email or accessing an online service still requires a network connection, even when the AI model itself remains on the Mac.

Perplexity recommends at least 36 GB of unified memory for running Computer locally, which exceeds the maximum available in some recent Apple silicon Macs. According to Apple's technical specifications, the standard M6 Mac mini starts with 16 GB and supports a maximum of 32 GB, falling short of Perplexity's recommendation.

The M5 Pro Mac mini can meet the recommendation with a 48 GB or 64 GB configuration. Meanwhile, the M5 Max Mac Studio starts with 36 GB, making it the less expensive of the two Mac Studio configurations that meets the recommendation without upgrades.

Older Apple Silicon Macs with sufficient memory can also qualify. Perplexity describes 36 GB as a recommendation rather than a strict minimum, so users with less memory aren't necessarily prevented from running the software.

The recommendation illustrates how memory capacity can determine which Macs are suitable for demanding local AI workloads. Larger models need enough space for their data while leaving resources available for macOS and other running apps.

Perplexity previously published inference benchmarks for Qwen 3.6 on an M5 Max MacBook Pro. Those tests don't show how complete Computer workflows perform across different Mac configurations, and Perplexity hasn't released comparable results.

Perplexity's expansion comes as Apple moves to tighten macOS privacy protections against autonomous AI agents. On October 2, Apple announced plans to strengthen Full Disk Access controls to prevent apps from exposing sensitive information without users fully understanding the risks.

Full Disk Access allows backup utilities to reach files that macOS ordinarily protects, but it can also expose emails, messages, browsing history, and other private information. The risks extend to people communicating with the Mac's owner, whose information could become accessible through those apps.

In a developer notice, Apple said future controls will require more explicit user action before granting such extensive access. The company hasn't announced when those changes will arrive, and it isn't eliminating Full Disk Access entirely.

Perplexity says Computer uses controlled permissions and isolated execution environments, but its announcement doesn't specify whether the local agent requires Full Disk Access.

Local AI processing reduces the need to send private data to remote servers, but it doesn't eliminate security risks. An agent can still mishandle sensitive files or follow malicious instructions embedded in documents.

The launch also gives Mac users another alternative to Siri AI, which uses on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute infrastructure for more demanding requests. Both systems can work with personal context and perform actions across apps, although their capabilities and underlying architectures differ.

items.title: Inside the iPhone Duo's groundbreaking hinge's innovations
items.content_html:
A YouTuber has taken a CT scan of the hinge on the iPhone Duo and uncovered both how it works and what its limitations are.

One of the surprises at the iPhone Duo launch was how it wasn't just built to either be fully open or fully closed. Instead, Apple has built it to offer different functions at many different angles.

According to testing done by HTX Studio on YouTube, iPhone Duo can stay open between 15 degrees and 145 degrees. If it's held below 15 degrees, magnets mean it will snap shut. Similarly, beyond 145 degrees, the screen will snap to fully open.

Apple has already said that its hinge contains almost 100 components. A CT scan of the hinge shows that this is concentrated in six sections, including two at the outer edges that are hinges connected to a central shaft.

Another section is a series of gears that are made so that rotating one side of the device also rotates the other. They stay in sync, they stay in lockstep, practically regardless of where you hold them.

Key to the design are two more sections immediately above and below the middle. These are a mix of springs and cams that either support or resist one another, depending on the angle of the screen.

"When the phone is fully open, the cams fit together, while the springs press against them to resist rotation, holding the foam until we apply enough force to fold it," says HTX Studio's video. "As we fold it, the cams compress the springs, which push back, and the resulting frictional torque overcomes the phone's own weight."

All of these sections are paired, with the same mechanical design at the top and bottom of the hinge. The final section is in the center, and seemingly features no moving parts.

Instead, it's the space through which flex cables connecting the two sides of the iPhone Duo can pass uninterrupted.

It's already been demonstrated by Apple that the iPhone Duo screen hides the crease in part through the ten layers of glass on the display. Plus it has a nanotexture display where all other foldables have glossy ones, meaning they practically highlight the crease in comparison.

But beyond that, this new CT scan also reveals the details of one hinge element where Apple does much the same as its rivals.

The top and bottom of the iPhone Duo hinge are mirror images of each other - image credit HTX Studio.

It's called the bending space and represents what radius the curved screen goes to.

"Think of the screen as a sheet of paper," says the video. "Fold it in half with a wide curve, and there won't be much of a crease when you open it, but press it flat with no room to bend, and you will get a very clear crease."

On the iPhone Duo, this bending space is 3.85mm at its widest point. That lies between the 3.8mm and 4.2mm of other unspecified but typical foldables.

Apple has achieved an IP68 rating for dust resistance, which is rare for a foldable, but still no reason to throw yours down on a beach. Nonetheless, it is something few rivals can match.

Similarly, most rivals reportedly have the same two small bumps at top and bottom of the crease that are there to protect their hinges. If dropped, such foldables can disperse the jolt to the metal sides of the phone instead of into the screen.

Apple's iPhone Duo does not have this and instead, the screen gets to be perfectly smooth all over. It's also able to do this because the entire hinge assembly is encased in a titanium cover for extra strength.

The iPhone Duo can support an Apple Pencil, but doing so means writing on the device's surface with a fairly hard-tipped device. HTX Studio, though, tested out not only an Apple Pencil but also regular pencils from 6B to 8H hardness, and tried them in a rig pressing down with a force of 100g.

There was a faintly visible mark on the display with a 6H pencil, but it wasn't apparent to the touch. At 8H, there were much more visible and touchable scratches.

But reportedly this is better than many rival foldables.

The video goes into more detail about the design and components that the CT scan revealed. The YouTubers did this on a review model, and, separately, other reviewers have put theirs through more real-world tests.
