items.title: Simplicity and Siri AI are the HomeView's killer features, says Apple
items.content_html:
The new Siri AI is the "magic" of HomeView, according to Apple execs, but part of that is how little users should have to interact with it.

HomeView is Apple's new $299 home hub device, and it was long rumored to be ready but waiting for Siri AI. Now that both that and the hardware are out, Apple has been stressing just how significant Siri AI is.

"With the magic of Siri AI, [HomeView] comes together in a way that we haven't been able to deliver before," Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home, told The Verge in a new interview.

That "magic" concerns in part how Siri AI has a more conversational understanding of how people speak. Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple, said that it's "great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way."

"As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way," she continued. "Because now it can be my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who's in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want."

Another part of Siri AI that is important yet doesn't get enough recognition is that it doesn't converse for the sake of it. Siri AI may be more conversational, but it is there to do a job for you.

"A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information," continued Rincon. "For us, it isn't about that. We're there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way."

Rincon leads product marketing and management for Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. She joined Apple from Google in March 2026.

Apple makes a persuasive case for how the HomeView avoids complexity, and doesn't try to be some kind of AI companion. HomeView has been designed for a particular type of user, or perhaps for the family of the right user.

Since it doesn't actually ship until November 13, 2026, there is still much to find out. But already the HomeView's limitations, intentional or not, are becoming apparent.

The chief one is that the screen is very small, especially for something Apple says can be wall mounted like a clock at the end of your kitchen. But then there is the fact that no apps can be run on HomeView, and so for common features like watching Apple TV, you have to AirPlay from your iPhone.

It's not clear that this element will ever be changed. But Apple is already reported to be working on a HomeView with a larger display.

items.title: iPhone camera and titanium chassis manufacturing expands in US
items.content_html:
Apple has announced new and extended partnerships with US firms to manufacture titanium for its iPhone enclosures and variable aperture technology for the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple's American Manufacturing Program (AMP) has already seen the company investing in firms across the country. One of those has been Qnity Electronics, and now Apple has announced that it is extending its partnership with this Delaware-based firm.

It's also revealed a new partnership with Pennsylvania's Perryman Company, a producer of titanium. Its titanium is to be used in the iPhone Duo and unspecified other devices.

"We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," said Sabih Khan, Apple's chief operating officer, in a statement. "American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro."

"We're proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support US jobs," he continued.

Apple says it will commit up to $100 million to the deal with Perryman over the next three years. The company melts, forges, and rolls titanium with a minimum of 80% recycled content for the iPhone Duo.

The expanded work with Qnity Electronics is said to specifically concern the new variable aperture camera now being used in the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple says that it now works with suppliers across all 50 states and that this supports over 450,000 American jobs.

This new announcement is a continuation of the initially $500 billion manufacturing investment announced in 2025. Apple has subsequently raised this figure to $600 billion, with the project set to run over four years.

Apple claims that almost 100 iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro components are being produced by companies in the US. These include long-time partner firms such as Corning, which is producing the iPhone's Ceramic Shield in Kentucky.

By the end of 2026, Corning's facility will reportedly be producing all of the cover glass for the iPhone and Apple Watch sold globally.

Then Apple CEO Tim Cook [middle] with Corning CEO Wendell Weeks [left] and CNBC's Jim Cramer [right] at Corning's facility in Kentucky - Image Credit: CNBC

As previously announced, Broadcom is expanding its radio frequency component production in Colorado. Coherent's Texas facility continues to provide components for Face ID and the Dynamic Island.

Then for processors, TSMC's Arizona fab is expected to produce over 100 million chips for Apple by the end of 2026. As TSMC continues to grow its Arizona campus, so Amkor Technology has begun construction for its packaging and test facility over in Peoria.

items.title: EU iPhone NFC concessions don't go far enough, says UK
items.content_html:
High fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions in the EU are said to be holding up wider third-party adoption of the NFC chip in an iPhone, and the UK is instead looking for easier access, and no cost.

Following both the UK's 2024 investigation into digital wallets, and Apple's agreement to open NFC access in Europe, the country's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) wants more. It argues that if Apple offers the same terms for UK developers, it will still be insufficient.

Consequently it wants easier access with fewer conditions. The CMA argues that none of this raises any security concerns, and that its proposals are needed to help UK businesses benefit from the technology.

"We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete," said Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA, in a statement. "By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services here — from payment apps and digital IDs to travel passes and digital keys."

The CMA notes that no firms have released an alternative to Apple Wallet in the UK, while five have in Europe. The first of those was Vipps, which launched in Norway in 2024.

According to the CMA, it is Apple's fees and access rules that are preventing rivals developing digital wallets. However, Apple has told AppleInsider and other venues that it disagrees with the UK's CMA.

"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections," said Apple in a statement. "We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

The CMA is currently presenting its proposals as a consultation. It is inviting comments until November 17, 2026, and says it will issue its decision shortly afterwards.

items.title: Apple still doesn't understand gamers in spite of iPhone being a gaming powerhouse
items.content_html:
An interview with the new App Store Worldwide head shows Apple is still playing by the same rulebook that fails to nail down what gamers want or need from a mobile platform.

If you've been following Apple long enough, you've heard this one before — Apple is finally serious about gaming. That's the mantra we've heard time and again from various product releases and Apple executives, but beyond financial success, it's hard to believe.

An interview conducted by Polygon with Apple's App Store Worldwide head Carson Oliver. The usual successes were listed, like having a Mac gaming app, powerful GPUs in Apple Silicon, and gaming-specific developer tools.

The thing is, Apple has always had a powerful platform for gaming on the iPhone. It is easily the most profitable gaming platform on Earth due to how many people own iPhones and pay for games.

However, very few gamers would consider iPhone, iPad, or especially Mac, a gaming platform. Sure, you can play games there, but they are the often derided "mobile" game.

Apple's previous attempts to address gamers have fallen flat, like the Apple Games app. Indie Games Week is the latest, and actually smart, move, but unless this is the start of a larger shift and not some one-time thing, nothing will change.

Today's mobile game is more advanced and beautifully rendered than ever. Call of Duty mobile's graphics rival previous-generation console shooters, while Genshin Impact feels like a game that shouldn't be able to exist on iPhone.

Some mobile games escape the stigma by being amazing experiences without the cruft

That is until you encounter your first loot box, gacha, or whatever scheme your game of choice is running.

Apple Arcade's promise was a great one that continues to shine through from time to time. Most of the games are direct ports of mobile games with ads and monetization stripped out.

The titles that stand out are the ones that could easily be found on a gaming console or in the Steam library. They're full games devoid of loot boxes or other schemes.

Yes, No Man's Sky is launching on iPhone and iPad in October, but that team already wanted to do that. Apple's technology made it possible, but I wouldn't herald this as some kind of victory or sign of more to come.

The interview shows a lot of contrasts and contradictions in Apple's game economy. Oliver touts iPhone's graphical prowess with the A20 Pro then mentions that the most popular games on the platform are indie titles that are predominantly pixel art.

Intensive graphics aren't a requirement to make a great game

"We've seen incredible growth of games coming to the App Store, in general, with more premium games releasing on the App Store this year than last," Oliver said. "While many of those are indies, we're also seeing more console and PC franchises coming to mobile, as it is a burgeoning audience for those games."

It sometimes feels like Apple is on the verge of getting it. Nintendo Switch has been so popular not because it's the most performant console on the market, but because its library is filled with fun and whimsical titles that don't need advanced GPUs to run.

He shares that popular games of the moment include Bolatro, Stardew Valley, Slay the Spire, and Bloons TD 6, which are all on Apple Arcade. That's nice and all, but I don't need an A20 Pro for those titles.

Gaming has seen a revival on iPhone thanks to Apple allowing emulators on the platform as well. However, Apple is shooting itself in the foot by not allowing more advanced emulators to run, like those that could emulate PlayStation 2 or Nintendo GameCube.

Apple's long history of gaming is filled with almosts and maybes. Every time it feels like they've figured it out, like with Angry Birds, Pokemon Go, and Infinity Blade, we end up with a race to the bottom.

There have even been multiple attempts to bring AAA games to iPhone, but they all fell flat. A lot of the reason behind these games flopping wasn't the price, execution, graphical fidelity, or anything relating to the games or hardware themselves.

'Death Stranding' works fine on iPad, but years late

The problem was, like many of Apple's efforts in gaming, too little too late with very little understanding of the gaming market. Those that wanted to play the Resident Evil 4 remake or Death Stranding already did years ago at full price on a console they owned.

What made matters worse is these games launched with an in-game purchase that was more expensive than what you could pay to get them on Steam or console. Many were even available as a part of a subscription like Xbox Game Pass or PlayStation Plus.

There's this movement in the gaming community asking for fewer games with worse graphics made by manageable team sizes that take longer to make a game. These ideals can be found in how much the gaming community latches onto indie darlings found on Steam.

'Cult of the Lamb' is a perfect example of what makes a great mobile game

Sure, there's always going to be a Grand Theft Auto VI or Elder Scrolls on the horizon that has everyone hyped. But, those games aren't on iPhone either.

Apple is trapped in this weird situation where it wants to be part of the conversation the way gaming consoles are, and wants a library as beloved as one on Steam, but it just never puts in the work. As has been exemplified again and again in the past decade, simply having game porting tools and powerful hardware isn't enough.

Game developers start with steam then port to consoles later. If a rare smartphone port happens, it's often a stripped-down version of the game filled with microtransactions or level selectors instead of linear storytelling.

My personal opinion is we need to get past "mobile," which demands addictive gameplay, monetization paths, microtransactions, and short gameplay loops. We also need to create a gaming platform on iPhone that can happily pay $7, $20, or even $60 for a title.

I'm serious. But make sure these games are available at full price at launch, not some years later when everyone has already played them elsewhere.

'Fantasian' proves that a full-length story-driven game can work on iPhone or iPad

The plague of "it has to be free then show loot boxes with premium passes" to succeed is killing us here. Stardew Valley is an amazing game because I can pay once, or get it on Apple Arcade, and play beginning to end without ever encountering an ad or microtransaction.

Fantasian, Hello Kitty Island Adventure, The Last Campfire, and plenty of others prove this is possible on iPhone. Embrace it, charge real money up front, and let me just play the game and get out of my way.

Sadly, Apple could never go that route because the cat is out of the bag. I'm afraid the only way that Apple can ever be serious about gaming is if it invents a time machine, goes back to when the App Store began, and encouraged game developers to charge real money for games.

There's a shift coming in the games industry thanks to AI-induced RAM and memory shortages. The PlayStation 6, if and when it ever releases, is estimated at over $1,000.

Games can survive generations regardless of graphic fidelity

It is making increasingly more sense to game on what you already own instead of investing in new hardware. Everyone owns a smartphone, and I expect we'll see a gaming-focused revolution on that front very soon.

The GameBoy, PlayStation Portable, and Nintendo DS were successful in spite of requiring specialized hardware to play expensive games that took upwards of 40 hours to complete. You can play many of those titles today thanks to emulation, which gaming companies seem allergic to finding a way to monetize.

My point is, your iPhone, iPad, and Mac are quite the capable gaming machines today. There are plenty of amazing titles you can play on them already, but Apple has an opportunity to make this a part of its brand.

Emulation lets us utilize existing hardware to explore classic games

Lean into it, find some developers and push to get their new pixel art-style game in the App Store. Promote one-time purchase games, rethink the App Store gaming page around what gamers actually want instead of what is most lucrative for Apple.

The real problem is Apple doesn't really need to change a thing, because regardless of gamer opinion on the matter, App Store games are among the most lucrative in the industry. It has to want to make a change for the better for gamers in spite of potential harm to revenue.

They're making money hand over fist because of mobile games preying on humanity's worst impulses. Gambling with loot boxes and paying to win are what define iPhone gaming, and unless Apple does something dramatic, it always will.

Let's see if Carson Oliver understands that and pushes Apple into finally getting serious about gaming. I wouldn't hold my breath.

items.title: There's 4K 144Hz HDMI support in these new USB-C hubs for as little as $39.99
items.content_html:
Plugable has introduced two USB-C hubs starting at $39.99 that bring 4K 144Hz HDMI output to compatible Macs, offering high-refresh-rate monitor support without a larger docking station.

The new Plugable USBC-6IN1 costs $39.99, while the USBC-8IN1E costs $59.99. Both hubs support a single external display at up to 4K 144Hz or 8K 30Hz through HDMI 2.1.

They also offer USB-C pass-through charging and don't require drivers on macOS, Windows, or ChromeOS. Previously, Plugable offered 4K 144Hz output only in its more expensive USBC-10IN1E hub.

The new models bring that capability to smaller, more affordable accessories. Mac users still need compatible hardware and macOS 26 or later to achieve the advertised refresh rates.

The $39.99 USBC-6IN1 offers HDMI 2.1, three USB-A ports, and one USB-C data port. All four USB data ports support speeds up to 5Gbps, while the USB-C port and one USB-A port can deliver up to 7.5W of power to connected devices.

The aluminum hub measures 4.79 inches long and includes a built-in 6.7-inch USB-C cable. It provides the essential connections for a monitor and USB accessories without adding Ethernet or memory card readers.

The $59.99 USBC-8IN1E adds Gigabit Ethernet and separate SD and microSD card readers. Both readers support UHS-I speeds up to 104MB/s and can operate simultaneously, allowing photographers to transfer files from two cards without swapping them.

The $59.99 USBC-8IN1E adds Gigabit Ethernet and separate SD and microSD card readers.

The USBC-8IN1E also includes a 5Gbps USB-C data port, a 5Gbps USB-A port, and a USB 2.0 port intended for wireless keyboard and mouse receivers. It measures 5.99 inches long and uses the same 6.7-inch integrated cable.

Both hubs support up to 100W of USB-C Power Delivery input, with a maximum of 85W passed through to the connected laptop. The remaining 15W is reserved for the hub and its ports, and neither model requires an external power adapter for basic operation.

Achieving 4K 144Hz or 8K 30Hz requires a Mac running macOS 26 or later with an M1 or M2 Pro or Max chip, or an M3 chip or newer. Users also need a compatible monitor and HDMI 2.1 cable.

Base M1 and M2 MacBooks, along with the MacBook Neo, are limited to 4K 60Hz through these hubs. Windows laptops require DisplayPort 1.4 with Display Stream Compression to reach the higher resolutions and refresh rates, while systems using DisplayPort 1.2 are limited to 4K 60Hz.

Each hub provides one HDMI output and doesn't increase the number of external displays a Mac can natively support.

Plugable lists the USBC-6IN1 and USBC-8IN1E for $39.99 and $59.99, respectively, with availability beginning October 20 through Amazon and Plugable's website. The company also advertises a 20% launch discount.

items.title: OLED iPad mini and touchscreen MacBook Pro: What to expect from Apple's second October event
items.content_html:
Apple has another release event, and this one is called "Pro and Tell." This is what will make an appearance on the day, including one very long-awaited MacBook Pro upgrade.

Fall has been unusually busy for Apple in 2026. After surprise Mac launches in late August and the usual September iPhone event, it's also launched smart home products in October.

But it's far from done. There's still more for it to launch.

Apple will hold the event on October 28. This would be the second event in the same month, making it one of the most intensive product-launch periods on record.

The event was confirmed by messages to invitees to an event called "Pro and tell." The name all but confirms changes to the MacBook Pro are on the way.

The invitation also includes an Apple logo, in what could be best described as an outline of a radar sweep. The colors used by the lines on the dark background are reminiscent of the MacBook Pro's usual colorways.

Can't wait to pro and tell next week. https://t.co/3wUkxwq35i

Greg Joswiak, aka "Joz," the SVP of Worldwide Marketing, also posted the logo to X, saying "Can't wait to pro and tell next week."

On when to expect to be able to get your hands on whatever Apple launches, a store refresh planned for November 6 may indicate when sales commence.

Entering the fall, Apple had a massive catalog of potential launches on its hands. A multi-launch slate of products was anticipated.

That has so far included the Mac mini and Mac Studio updates in August as an early surprise launch.

Apple launched a lot during its September 9 "Surprise and Shine" event, including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and the fifth-generation AirPods.

The first October event was all about the smart home, with updates made to the Apple TV 4K and the HomePod mini 2. There was also the introduction of the HomeView and a bunch of related smart home device launches to match.

That sheer quantity of product launches is enough for any normal year, but there are still some candidates for launch. That launched items list doesn't have any iPad products, nor does it include any portable Mac models, which are now expected for this new event.

iPad mini

Back in September, it had a good chance of launching alongside the iPhones, but the iPad mini update is still expected to arrive. Based on the current state of rumors that would be the late October event.

One way of knowing it's on the way is from a French regulatory website. An identifier was found that related to the iPad mini, practically confirming the model's imminent arrival.

The eighth-generation device's main change is anticipated to be the display. An 8.4-inch LTPS panel with hybrid OLED should bring it in line with the iPad Pro range, if not to the same standard of specifications.

While brighter and more vibrant, the display won't necessarily have ProMotion, typically a Pro model feature. However, as usual for the rumor mill, that is still up for debate.

iPad mini on an arm

Beyond the display, you can also count on a chip upgrade. The current favorite is the A20, along with the possible inclusion of Apple's networking and modem chips.

Smaller changes that have been rumored include a repositioning of the FaceTime camera, as well as a new vibration-based speaker to help improve water resistance.

OLED MacBook Pro

One of the big-hitter rumors for the MacBook Pro line has been the display. An OLED-equipped model has been rumored a long time, and it seems like it'll finally arrive.

Forecasts previously put a launch at early 2027, but it's now thought to take place in October. Or at least to be announced in October with a release in November.

That seems to match the late event rumors quite well.

An OLED display produces a more vibrant image with high levels of contrast, while also saving power. As a touchscreen, it will also be the first MacBook to be touch-enabled, and join a notebook market that already has many touch-enabled displays.

On October 5, references were found in the macOS 27.2 developer beta, indicating multiple applications were set up to receive additional touch recognition capabilities. This is probably an inadvertent confirmation from Apple that it's on the way.

You can probably expect it to be a spec-bump update beyond the display, including using Apple's newer chips.

There may be a change in construction that helps it lose weight. On October 4, a report claimed there will be a significant weight reduction, thanks to Apple redesigning components to be smaller and lighter.

However, an October 8 report walked back earlier claims that there would be a chassis upgrade that made it thinner.

M6 MacBook Pro and iMac

Following the surprise launches of the M6 Mac mini and updated Mac Studio in late August, the prospect of spec-bump updates to other Mac models was good. While everyone will be looking at the new OLED model, other entry-level models are still a possibility.

The most obvious ones that have been rumored about are the M6 models. There are M6 models of MacBook Pro and iMac allegedly on the horizon, catching up to the M6 Mac mini.

The current 24-inch iMac.

The entry-level M6 MacBook Pro rumors say that it will still use a mini LED screen with ProMotion. It'll also use an identical six-speaker sound system, the same ports, and the same chassis as the current generation.

However, it will instead get an upgrade to the M6 chip, making it a typical Apple spec-bump upgrade.

It's a similar story for the M6 24-inch iMac, with it also thought to be given a speed boost, but retain the current design. An overhaul with OLED is expected for the iMac at some point, but that will be far into the future.

For now, any iMac upgrade will keep the display as-is.

What appears above is what we expect Apple to show during the late October event. There's even more waiting in the wings, but they're rumored to be arriving at a later time, in early 2027.

That list includes updates to:

As always, AppleInsider will keep tabs on the rumor mill and potential launches in the future.

items.title: Taction won record-breaking $5.7 billion verdict against Apple, asks for more
items.content_html:
Taction hopes that the court will award additional damages for iPhone and Apple Watch sales made in 2026 in addition to hundreds of millions in prejudgment interest.

Even as Apple challenges the $5.7 billion verdict set by a jury in the Taction patent case, the company hopes to squeeze out more. A jury ruled that Apple violated two patents, though not willingly, and Apple denied any wrongdoing.

According to a report from Reuters, Taction has asked a federal judge for hundreds of millions more in payment from Apple. It argues that the damages only cover from 2021 to March 2026 and should cover the previous six months as well.

Taction has also asked for prejudgment interest at California's 7% statutory rate. The interest on $5.7 billion would be an incredible figure on top of the already large sum.

The argument is simple. Taction says "the size of the jury's award is no reason to withhold interest."

Of course, Apple plans to appeal and has already challenged the jury's verdict. It was allegedly made without any materials to accurately determine the damages payment.

Plus, the logic of the case and the alleged infringement are contradictory. Apple hopes it can have the whole thing thrown out with a summary judgment, but no verdict has been shared yet.

With the tvOS 27.2 and HomePod Software 27.2 release candidates, Apple has added support for surround sound on the 2026 Apple TV 4K and for Sound Glow on select HomePods.

On October 13, as part of its "Welcome Home" event, Apple's streaming box and smallest smart speaker received meaningful hardware upgrades. A new surround sound option is also available when you pair the latest Apple TV 4K with four HomePod mini 2 units.

Alternatively, it's also possible to use four HomePod 2 speakers, or two HomePod mini 2 units and a pair of HomePod 2 speakers for the surround sound experience. Meanwhile, the HomePod Software 27.2 release candidate extends Apple's new Sound Glow feature to the HomePod 2 and original HomePod mini. With Sound Glow, the top of compatible HomePod models pulses colors that match the audio being played.

items.title: Apple's latest design showcase explores how furniture can inspire us to stay present
items.content_html:
Apple's latest design showcase uses familiar objects to explore how people connect with their surroundings and each other.

Apple's second Designers of Tomorrow showcase brings four emerging design practices to Design Miami Paris. This year's Design for Presence theme explores how physical objects encourage attention, reflection, and interaction.

Curator Rodman Primack heads the exhibition, which Wallpaper* previewed ahead of its opening. Participants used Apple tools, including iPad, Apple Pencil, and MacBook Pro, to develop their work.

Image credit: Apple

Egyptian-Danish architect Salem S. Charabi created "The Eminence of Light" using materials found around his Cairo studio. The lantern combines a limestone base, a banana paper diffuser, and interlocking date palm fronds.

"For this project, every component had to be mapped out in detail. I sketched and did all the 3D modelling on my MacBook Pro. It was a complex process getting everything to fit just right — from the carving of the stone and the paper moulds, down to the delicate base."

Brooklyn designer Isabel Rower based "The Padded Chair 1860" on a historic chair she photographed in Paris. Its fringe contains over 1,500 ceramic beads, designed to produce an appealing sound when brushed.

"A few years ago I took a photograph of a boudoir chair from the 1860s in the Musee des Arts Decoratifs in Paris. I found the form highly unconventional and I was drawn to its dramatic fringed skirt. When faced with the prompt of 'Design for Presence', I felt that this chair was the perfect object to revisit."

Seoul artist Yoonjeong Lee's "New Form" combines a wooden table with an integrated lamp. Roughly 5,000 veneer sheets form its base, while three worn pencils secure the paper lampshade.

"One day, I was looking at a pencil that was almost used up, and I noticed its shape looked like a nail," she told Wallpaper*. "A pencil doesn't disappear as it wears down. It stays on in a new form: as a letter, as knowledge, as music. For me, it stayed on as a nail."

Mexican studio Parafernalia developed "MonoAmbiente 1", a folding table with two stools that nest beneath it. Its acid-etched stainless steel surfaces form a continuous landscape when the furniture is closed.

"Conversation is rarely an isolated activity. We talk while we play, eat, drink, walk, or cook. In this piece, the accompanying activities create the conditions for dialogue rather than defining it," the designers said of the piece. "The deployment of the piece marks a shift from solitary observation to shared occupation, from looking to participating."

The exhibition runs October 21 through October 25, 2026, at Hotel de Maisons in Paris.

items.title: Release candidates of iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 land as release nears
items.content_html:
The first release candidates for iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, and macOS 27.2 have arrived for testing.

The first release candidates for iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, and HomePod Software 27.2 have surfaced, following four developer beta cycles, three for tvOS 27.2 and HomePod Software 27.2.

While a release candidate or RC version means the update is practically at the state it will be distributed to the general public, there's no guarantee it will be the only one. A second RC is always a possibility.

The first major post-milestone update is normally a point-one version, which unusually isn't the case this time. As the iOS 27.1 build is designated to be used with the iPhone Duo, that version is being skipped for the non-foldable iPhone models.

The new 27.2 builds are:

Apple has also released RC builds for older operating systems:

The RC round arrives after the fourth developer betas, which were distributed on October 5. However, while there were builds for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and visionOS, the round didn't include builds for tvOS nor HomePod Software.

The third round was shared by Apple on October 5. The second appeared on September 21, and the first round landed on September 16.

The first round introduced a few changes to iOS 27.2, including a redesigned Health app, which works alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12.

FaceTime gained dual capture support, Siri AI added localization for multiple languages, and Apple TV profiles from tvOS 26.2 came over to the iPhone.

The second build had indications of a new AutoLock security feature, which locks down an iPhone if it is detected to have been snatched or otherwise stolen from the owner. The feature isn't accessible to testers, but it was spotted as running in the background in a non-functional manner.

The fourth iOS 27.2 beta had Apple Music change its icon to black and white, as well as a withdrawal of the redesign of the Apple Health app in favor of a later release. HomePods also gained a new setting to Lock Controls.

AppleInsider warns readers trying out beta software should do so on secondary, spare hardware instead of their mission-critical or daily driver devices. There is always a risk of buggy, broken, or other potentially harmful elements in beta software, which can be a risk to your data.

Members of the public should seek out the public betas instead of the developer versions as safer alternatives. In either case, it is also advisable to keep up-to-date backups on hand.
